name: Exposure Fusion Trace
description: Detects traces of exposure fusion processing — verifies whether multi-exposure blending follows optical principles.
mechanism:
This method detects whether an image was created through exposure fusion (multi-exposure blending) and verifies if the fusion follows physically plausible optical principles:

1. **Dynamic Range Analysis**: The method measures the local dynamic range across overlapping 64×64 blocks by computing the ratio of the 95th to 5th percentile luminance values. Exposure-fused images show extended local dynamic range (>8 EV) that exceeds what a single exposure can capture, yet the pixel values remain within the standard 8-bit or 16-bit range (unlike true HDR files).

2. **Exposure Consistency Map**: For genuine multi-exposure fusion (e.g., Mertens et al., 2007), each pixel originates from the best-exposed source image. The method estimates the source exposure for each pixel region by inverting the camera response function and computing the implied exposure time. In authentic fusions, these implied exposures cluster around 3–5 discrete EV values. AI-generated pseudo-HDR images show a continuous distribution of implied exposures, as neural networks do not follow the discrete multi-shot capture process.

3. **Weight Map Reconstruction**: The Mertens exposure fusion algorithm uses weight maps based on contrast, saturation, and well-exposedness metrics. The method attempts to reconstruct plausible weight maps by decomposing the final image into hypothetical source exposures. Authentic fusions produce smooth, region-coherent weight maps, while AI-generated images yield fragmented, noisy weight maps indicating they were not created through genuine multi-exposure blending.

4. **Ghost Artifact Detection**: Multi-exposure fusion from handheld shots or scenes with motion produces characteristic ghosting artifacts at object boundaries. The method searches for translucent duplicate edges with spatial offsets consistent with inter-frame alignment errors. The presence of physically plausible ghosting provides positive evidence of genuine multi-exposure capture.
parameters:
Block size: 64×64 pixels for dynamic range analysis
Exposure clusters: 3–7 discrete EV levels expected
Weight map smoothness threshold: gradient variance < 0.5
Ghost detection: translucent edge search with 1–15 pixel offset range
Dynamic range threshold: > 8 EV for fusion detection
Minimum image size: 512×512 pixels
accuracy: 77–85% accuracy in distinguishing genuine exposure fusion from AI-generated pseudo-HDR content. Exposure consistency analysis achieves 82% on multi-exposure datasets. Ghost artifact detection provides 90% positive identification when ghosting is present. Performance drops to 70% on tripod-captured fusions with perfect alignment (no ghosting).
source: Mertens, T., Kautz, J., & Van Reeth, F. (2007). Exposure Fusion. Pacific Graphics, 382–390.
useCase: Verifying whether HDR-like images were created through genuine multi-exposure capture or AI generation. Detecting AI-generated landscape and architectural photographs that simulate wide dynamic range. Authenticating real-estate and insurance photographs claimed to show accurate lighting conditions.
strengths:
• Exploits the fundamental difference between discrete multi-shot capture and continuous AI generation
• Weight map analysis provides interpretable forensic evidence
• Ghost artifact detection is a strong positive authentication signal
• Effective on landscape, architectural, and interior photography
• Can identify the specific fusion algorithm used (Mertens, Debevec, exposure bracketing)
limitations:
• Single-shot HDR (computational photography in smartphones) may not show multi-exposure signatures
• Tripod-mounted fusions with perfect alignment are harder to verify
• Heavy tone mapping can mask fusion artifacts
• AI models trained on HDR datasets may better approximate fusion characteristics
• Requires full-resolution images — resized thumbnails lose subtle fusion traces
